children.text: Once a riverside villa of the Spanish governor-general, this palace is now the residence of the Philippine president. The main building is a working office and closed to visitors, but the heritage mansions inside the palace complex let you see the Presidential Museum for free on a booked tour or as a walk-in.

Malacañang Palace (officially Malacañan Palace) is the residence and workplace of the President of the Philippines, standing on the north bank of the Pasig River in the San Miguel district of Manila. The name is so symbolic that in Philippine news "Malacañang" alone simply means the Office of the President. There are several theories about its origin; the best known says it comes from the Tagalog Mamalakáya-han, "the place where fishermen live."
The palace began in
as a riverside summer villa built by the Spanish aristocrat Luis José de la Rocha. The government bought it in
as the governor-general's summer residence, and after the

earthquake destroyed the governor's palace in Intramuros, the governor-general moved here and it became the official residence. It remained the governor's residence under American rule and became the presidential residence when the Commonwealth government was established in
. It was extensively rebuilt in
, and during the
People Power Revolution citizens entered the palace and discovered Imelda Marcos's enormous shoe collection, a scene still famous around the world.
The palace complex includes the main building, Kalayaan Hall built in

, the administrative Mabini Hall, and Malacañang Park across the river. Its white buildings blend the bahay na bato style (traditional Filipino stone-and-wood houses) with neoclassicism, and are known for arched loggias and wooden lattice windows. Kalayaan Hall once housed the Presidential Museum and Library and offered public tours, but it is no longer part of the official visitor information and now serves, like the main building, as working office space.

The places travelers can actually enter are the "Malacañang Heritage Mansions," clustered on General Solano Street and J.P. Laurel Street on the west side of the complex. The Office of the President restored these 19th-century mansions and opened them as museums on
June 1, 2023

, and you can visit Teus Mansion, now the Presidential Museum, and Bahay Ugnayan for free. They suit travelers interested in modern Philippine history and the stories of past presidents, as well as anyone looking for a free indoor sight to escape the heat or rain. Visits are running as of
, but since these are Office of the President facilities, schedules can change, so check the latest notices before you go.
Built around

, this was the home of Spanish businessman Valentín Teus, who acquired the distillery that grew into today's Tanduay rum company. It now displays clothing, campaign materials, gifts and photos of every president from Emilio Aguinaldo to Rodrigo Duterte, along with national symbols such as the flag, the national seal and presidential regalia.
Teus Mansion brings together in one room portraits of past first ladies commissioned in
. Comparing how dresses and hairstyles changed over the decades is part of the fun, making it a must-see alongside the presidential galleries.

This is where guided tours begin. The museum traces the life of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. from his birth and school years through his entry into politics to his inauguration, using timelines, photos and infographics, and the old mansion itself, with its iron gate and red roof, is worth a look.
Bought in
by French businessman Michael Goldenberg, the mansion was purchased by Imelda Marcos in

, who had National Artist Leandro Locsin restore it. It is now a cultural events venue and its interior is usually closed, but on days without events you can see its facade with lace-like eaves and a fountain.
Visitors receive a free "museum passport" and get a stamp at each mansion. Children stay entertained collecting stamps, and it makes a nice travel souvenir.

You cannot enter the main building or Kalayaan Hall, but the white pillars, iron fence and tree-shaded sidewalk of J.P. Laurel Street convey the atmosphere of the palace complex. Freedom Park in front of the palace has a dove-topped monument commemorating the
liberation of Manila. This is a security zone, so follow the guards' instructions where walking or photography is restricted.

children.text: The palace was originally built facing the river. Ride the free Pasig River Ferry run by the MMDA upstream from the Escolta side, and you pass the restricted riverfront zone in front of the palace and see the complex from the water. November–April
dry season is most comfortable. Mornings and evenings are relatively cool especially in

During the

rainy season, showers and typhoons are frequent, and in major typhoons the Pasig River has risen enough to flood the area around the palace. On the other hand, the indoor visit makes a good rainy-day alternative. The mansions are closed on Mondays and holidays, so many days during Holy Week (the week before Easter) and the Christmas and year-end holidays are closed; check the calendar first.

San Miguel, where the palace stands, is a district of government offices and universities, so there is almost no tourist accommodation. Staying at a mid-range or budget hotel in Ermita or Malate about
3–4km

away, or in Binondo, puts you a short Grab ride away, and many travelers stay in Makati or BGC and come for a half day. If you have booked a morning tour, staying nearby is less stressful given rush-hour traffic.

Food and drinks are not allowed inside the mansions, so eat before or after your visit. Nearby Mendiola Street and the university belt have many cheap Filipino home-style eateries (carinderias) popular with students, where you can have adobo, sinigang and a plate of rice without spending much. The market around Quiapo Church is good for snacks such as turon (fried banana rolls) and kakanin (rice cakes), and in the evening we recommend crossing to Binondo Chinatown for dumplings and stir-fried noodles.
For a guided tour, apply through the
official tour request form
at least 3 working days (excluding Mondays, Tuesdays and holidays) before your visit, and go only after you receive approval.
Guided tours start at

Official sources list the opening days differently, as "Thursday–Sunday" and "Tuesday–Sunday." The mansions are closed on Mondays and holidays, so if you plan to go on a Tuesday or Wednesday, confirm by phone or email first.
This is a presidential compound with security screening. Bring a photo ID (a passport for foreigners) and keep to one small bag to get through security faster.
The official rule is to "dress respectfully and appropriately." It is safest to avoid slippers, sleeveless tops and short shorts.
Video recording is strictly prohibited inside the mansions, and food and drinks are not allowed. Take photos only as staff permit.
Children must be at least 5 years old and accompanied by a parent or guardian. Guided tours take a maximum of 25 people per slot, so groups should apply early.
If you drive, parking inside the palace complex is first come, first served. Walk-in visitors are not provided with a guide or the shuttle within the complex.
San Sebastian Church and Quiapo Church are close by, making this easy to combine into a half-day route through northern downtown Manila.
The area around the palace is a presidential security zone. Do not enter areas blocked by guards, do not photograph checkpoints or security personnel, and do not fly drones.

The main palace building and Kalayaan Hall are not open to the public. Parts of the complex open only during occasional events, so do not show up based on old online information about "Kalayaan Hall museum tours."
Visits may be suddenly canceled or rescheduled because of the president's schedule, state events or typhoons. Check the official information again the day before your visit.
Mendiola Street in front of the palace is a frequent rally site. On protest days roads may be blocked, so take a detour and stay away from crowds.
Quiapo and the market lanes are crowded and pickpocketing is common. Keep your phone and wallet in a bag worn in front.
During the
June–October
rainy season, heavy rain can flood the roads around the palace. Check the weather forecast and closure notices first.
